data.sourceWord: Angels influence — accountability and good deeds
data.targetWord: Belief in recording angels influences Muslims to remain constantly God-conscious, avoiding sin because every action is recorded and will be judged. It motivates them to perform good deeds.
Jibril's revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad means Muslims revere angels as conveyors of divine guidance; this influences them to study and follow the Qur'an as the authentic word of God.

data.sourceWord: Qur'an — direct word of Allah, unaltered
data.targetWord: Muslims believe the Qur'an is the direct, final and unaltered word of Allah. Uthman standardised one written version to prevent change. It is an infallible source of authority coming directly from God.

data.sourceWord: Qur'an — guidance for the Day of Judgement
data.targetWord: The Qur'an is a source of guidance from Allah to help Muslims lead good lives in preparation for the Day of Judgement. It covers belief, worship, ethics, law and community life comprehensively.
'Read in the name of your Lord.' (96:1) — the first words revealed to Muhammad by Jibril, establishing the Qur'an as a divine command to read and reflect on God's revelation.

data.question: Which festival marks the end of Ramadan?

data.targetWord: Salah five times daily is the second pillar of Islam. It involves ritual purity (wudu), facing Makkah, and performing set positions (rakat) with specific recitations, maintaining constant awareness of Allah.

Du'a (personal supplication) allows Muslims to speak directly to Allah at any time. Unlike the formal Salah, du'a is spontaneous and personal, expressing gratitude, need, or praise in the believer's own words.
The mosque is the centre of Islamic community life, providing a place for the five daily prayers, the Friday Jumu'ah prayer, Islamic education, and social support for the community.

data.sourceWord: Mosque — contrasting views on women's access
data.targetWord: Some traditional mosques restrict women to separate areas or do not encourage their attendance, while many modern mosques actively welcome women and provide equal facilities for men and women.

Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. Muslims attend Eid prayers, wear new clothes, give Zakat ul-Fitr (charity before prayer) and celebrate with family, expressing gratitude to Allah for strength to fast.

Id-ul-Adha commemorates Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God. Animals are sacrificed and the meat shared with the poor, family, and neighbours. Hajj pilgrims celebrate it at Mina.
'And when they had both submitted their wills to God, and he had laid him prostrate on his forehead, We called out to him: O Ibrahim! Thou hast already fulfilled the vision.' (37:103-104)

data.title: Angels in Islamic Belief
data.sourcePassage: Belief in angels (mala'ika) is one of the six articles of faith in Sunni Islam. Angels are created from light and are sinless, carrying out God's commands without question. The greatest angel is Jibril (Gabriel), who revealed the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad over 23 years beginning in the cave of Hira. Mika'il (Michael) is associated with mercy, sustenance and reward. Israfil will blow the trumpet to signal the Day of Judgement. The Angel of Death (Azra'il) takes the souls of the dying. Two angels, Munkar and Nakir, question the dead in the grave about their faith. The Kiraman Katibin are two recording angels who accompany every person, writing down their good and bad deeds in a Book of Deeds. On the Day of Judgement, each person will be given their Book of Deeds to read. For Muslims, belief in angels reinforces awareness of God's presence, motivates ethical behaviour, and confirms that every action has eternal significance.
